Picture a jet engine bolted to the ceiling to move a bit of air. That's how most of us are still using AI.

Ask a question, get an answer, copy it into an email, move on. It's useful. It's also the smallest thing the technology does.

The real difference shows up when AI runs the whole path instead of one step of it: it reads the incoming email, works out what it is, routes it, drafts the reply in your voice, and books the follow-up. Your job shrinks to a yes or a no.

Same tools everyone already has. The gap isn't the model — it's whether you gave it the full job or just a question.

Most clients don't leave because the work was bad. They leave because, three weeks in, they quietly stopped feeling sure they made the right call.

That gap — between the day someone signs and the day they actually feel confident — is where you keep them or lose them. And for most of us it's still held together by memory. A welcome email here, a kickoff call someone promised, an intake form we'll chase "once things calm down."

Nothing dramatic breaks. It just adds up to a first month that feels less polished than the pitch that won them.

The founders getting the most out of AI this year aren't the ones who automated the most. They're the ones who automated the right layer.

Most of your day is glue. Copying a number from one tab into another. Chasing the person who owes you a reply. Reformatting notes into an update nobody reads carefully. Routing a message to whoever handles that. None of it needs you — it just needs doing, and it quietly eats the hours when you'd actually think.

That's the layer to hand over. The status updates, the tagging, the chasing, the first draft of everything. Give the machine the glue.

Thorough and slow look the same from the inside.

A lot of German B2B teams pride themselves on being careful — detailed proposals, proper relationship-building, nothing rushed. Good. But look at the operational layer underneath, and a lot of "careful" is just manual: pulling lead lists by hand, writing every follow-up from scratch, rebuilding the same report every fortnight.

That isn't thoroughness. It's drag. And it compounds every week.

Everyone waiting for their big launch is quietly avoiding the small one they could ship today.

For years I thought building meant working toward a moment — the reveal, the announcement, the day it all goes live and the room finally claps. So I saved things up. Polished in private. Waited until it felt worthy of a launch.
